query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: By integrating a computational free‐energy sampling method with high‐throughput screening of process parameters (such as temperature ramp rates, dwell times, and cooling profiles), it is possible to kinetically bypass the thermodynamic barrier caused by the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu. This approach will promote a large‐scale reaction that yields a stable, homogeneous composite microstructure suitable for high-temperature nuclear reactor applications.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite precursor consisting of mixed elemental refractory powders and Cu (or Cu-alloy) particles, where traditional processing leads to phase separation due to positive heat of mixing.
generation.intervention: Apply a computational free‐energy sampling method to map out the metastable reaction pathways and then use high‐throughput experimental screening to adjust processing parameters (temperature ramp rates, dwell times, cooling profiles) accordingly.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled high-temperature conditions that mimic the reactor operating environment, using rapid, pressure-assisted or laser-based methods for in-situ alloying at large scales.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined microstructure with reduced segregation of Cu; formation of a kinetically stabilized interface between Cu and the refractory matrix
generation.mechanism: The free‐energy sampling identifies metastable reaction pathways that bypass or suppress the kinetic drivers of Cu segregation. The optimized processing parameters then lock in the desired homogeneous microstructure before phase separation can occur.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite material exhibiting a more uniform distribution of Cu within the refractory high‐entropy alloy matrix, with suppressed phase separation, enhanced interfacial integrity, and improved stability under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing methods (e.g., traditional blending, casting, or standard powder metallurgy) typically yield coarse, multiphase microstructures with significant Cu segregation due to the positive heat of mixing.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this method may depend on the precise control of processing parameters; scaling to extreme or variable reactor conditions might require further tuning of the reaction pathway and parameter space.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by trends in free‐energy based methods and rapid processing techniques, the exact processing window and parameter values required are not yet established and will need detailed experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of composite samples using refractory high‐entropy alloy powders mixed with Cu. Process these samples under a matrix of conditions determined by the free‐energy sampling predictions (varying temperature ramp rates, dwell times, and cooling profiles). Characterize the as-processed microstructures using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to assess Cu segregation and phase uniformity. Perform high-temperature stability tests under simulated reactor conditions.
measurements: Degree of Cu segregation (via EDX mapping)
Mechanical properties at high temperature (yield strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed using the free‐energy guided parameter set do not show a statistically significant improvement in microstructural uniformity (i.e., reduced Cu segregation) and high-temperature stability compared to samples processed via conventional methods, then the hypothesis that the integrated free‐energy sampling and high‐throughput screening method enables formation of a stable composite microstructure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Unfortunately, elements Al, Cr, and Si very easily form brittle intermetallic compounds with other refractory

Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. Here, we propose a highly efficient DFT-based method aided by a specially designed machine learning potential. As the machine learning potential can closely reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, even for multi-component alloys, the costly thermodynamic integration can be fully substituted with more efficient free energy perturbation calculations. The method achieves overall savings of computational resources by 80% compared to current alternatives. We apply the method to the high-entropy alloy TaVCrW and calculate its melting properties

decision.trend: Early work in refractory high‐entropy alloys shifted from conventional casting and arc melting -- which often resulted in coarse and multiphase microstructures due to thermodynamic challenges -- to advanced powder‐metallurgy techniques. Studies using mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering demonstrated that applying rapid, pressure‐assisted processing can refine grain sizes and help stabilize the microstructure. Subsequent work using additive manufacturing methods (such as selective laser melting and laser powder bed fusion) further showed that high-energy, rapid processing can yield finer, more homogeneous microstructures. However, while these methods successfully control phase formation in many refractory systems, they have not fully resolved the fundamental challenge posed by a significant positive heat of mixing with Cu in composite formulations.
decision.unsolved: The open question remains how to achieve a large‐scale, reactive processing method that not only drives the formation of a homogeneously reacted composite but also avoids phase separation due to the high positive enthalpy of mixing between refractory elements and Cu.
decision.lever: Implement a computational free‐energy sampling approach coupled with high‐throughput process parameter screening (e.g., tuning temperature ramp rates, dwell times, and cooling profiles) to identify reaction pathways that kinetically bypass or suppress Cu segregation.
decision.why: Given the evolving trend from traditional to high-energy, rapid processing methods to achieve refined microstructures in refractory alloys, leveraging a free‐energy scheme will directly address the thermodynamic barrier by pinpointing metastable reaction routes. This approach is well suited to tailor the processing window for large-scale reactions and can guide experimental validations for stable composite formation despite the positive heat of mixing challenge.
